subject: biology

items.q: Which statement describes the roles of RNA polymerase in transcription?
items.correct: It separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides, positioned by pairing with the template strand, into one RNA strand.
items.misconception: It links RNA nucleotides into a strand once helicase has opened the DNA and a primer has been laid down.
items.why: Students learn the replication machinery (helicase, primase, DNA polymerase) first and assume that any process opening the helix needs the same set of enzymes; the two polymerases have similar names, so the limitations of DNA polymerase are transferred to RNA polymerase. RNA polymerase has several roles in transcription: it binds to the DNA, separates the two strands, positions RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and links them by covalent bonds. No helicase and no primer are needed.
items.specStatementText: Transcription: RNA polymerase makes an RNA copy of one gene
items.random_wrong: It copies both DNA strands of the gene at the same time, producing a double-stranded RNA molecule from the gene.

items.q: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?
items.correct: AUGCGUA
items.misconception: UACGCAU
items.why: Transcription is described as 'copying' the gene, and the everyday meaning of a copy is something identical. Students also forget that the strand read by the enzyme is the template, so they expect the product to match it rather than to match the other strand. RNA nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing with the template strand, so the RNA is complementary to the template. It matches the sequence of the other DNA strand of the gene, with uracil in place of thymine.
items.specStatementText: Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
items.random_wrong: UAGCGAU

items.q: During transcription, what holds each RNA nucleotide in position against the DNA template strand while it is being added to the growing RNA?
items.correct: Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, which break again when the RNA is released.
items.misconception: Covalent bonds made by RNA polymerase between the RNA base and the DNA base opposite it.
items.why: Students know that an enzyme is involved and that enzymes make and break bonds, so they assume the enzyme bonds the RNA to the DNA. They also see 'RNA polymerase joins nucleotides' and picture the join as being to the template rather than to the previous RNA nucleotide. Complementary bases pair by hydrogen bonds that form and break easily. RNA polymerase forms covalent bonds between the sugar of one RNA nucleotide and the phosphate of the next, building the RNA backbone, and the finished RNA separates from the DNA as the hydrogen bonds break.
items.specStatementText: Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen bonds between identical bases, so the RNA is an exact copy of the template.

items.q: A neuron formed before birth does not divide again, yet it transcribes the same genes throughout a lifetime of many decades. Which statement explains how this is possible?
items.correct: Transcription reads the template strand without altering its base sequence, so the sequence is conserved for life.
items.misconception: Each round of transcription slightly alters the template, so the neuron periodically replicates its DNA to restore the gene.
items.why: In everyday use a template or stencil is something that can wear out, and students picture the RNA nucleotides being taken from the DNA rather than paired with it. Replication and transcription are learned together, so replication is imagined as a repair process for transcribed genes. Single DNA strands can be used as a template for transcribing a base sequence without the DNA base sequence changing. The RNA nucleotides come from the nucleoplasm, pair with the template by hydrogen bonds and then leave as part of the RNA; the template itself is unchanged.
items.specStatementText: A DNA template can be read again and again without changing
items.random_wrong: Because the neuron does not replicate its DNA again, its base sequences need not be conserved and can change freely.

items.q: Developing red blood cells produce large amounts of the beta chain of haemoglobin, but liver cells produce none, although both cell types contain the gene. Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: The gene is transcribed in developing red blood cells but not in liver cells, so liver cells make no mRNA for the protein.
items.misconception: Liver cells lost the gene when they differentiated, so they no longer contain the DNA sequence for the beta chain.
items.why: Differentiation is described as cells 'becoming different', and the simplest picture is that they end up with different DNA. Students have also met the loss of the nucleus by red blood cells and generalize the idea of losing genetic material. All somatic cells of an organism contain the same genes. Cells differ because different genes are transcribed in different cell types; transcription is the first stage of gene expression and is a key stage at which a gene is switched on or off.
items.specStatementText: Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
items.random_wrong: Both cell types transcribe the gene, but only red blood cells translate the mRNA into the beta chain polypeptide.

items.q: Why is transcription regarded as a key stage at which the expression of a gene can be switched on or off?
items.correct: It is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and no polypeptide.
items.misconception: Every gene in a cell is transcribed and translated all the time, so expression is not switched on or off at any stage.
items.why: DNA is introduced as 'the instructions for the cell', and instructions are assumed to be carried out. The idea that a cell contains a full set of genes and uses only some of them is not needed until gene expression is studied. Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. A gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and no polypeptide, so a cell's proteins depend on which of its genes are being transcribed.
items.specStatementText: Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
items.random_wrong: All genes in a cell are transcribed at all times, so expression is switched on and off only at translation.

items.q: What happens during translation?
items.correct: The base sequence of an mRNA molecule is used to determine the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.
items.misconception: A base sequence of DNA is used as a template to make a complementary mRNA molecule inside the cell nucleus.
items.why: The two words look and sound alike and are always taught as a pair. In everyday English 'translation' means converting between languages and 'transcription' means writing something out, and students do not connect these meanings to which molecule is made at each stage. Transcription writes out the gene in the same language (nucleotide bases) as RNA. Translation converts the mRNA base sequence into a different language, the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.
items.specStatementText: Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
items.random_wrong: Ribosomes convert the bases of the mRNA into amino acids, which are then joined into a chain.

items.q: Which statement about the binding of mRNA and tRNA to a ribosome is correct?
items.correct: The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and two tRNAs can bind to the large subunit at the same time.
items.misconception: The mRNA binds to the large subunit, because it is the larger molecule, and the tRNAs bind to the small subunit.
items.why: Students match sizes: the long mRNA is assigned to the large subunit and the small tRNAs to the small subunit. Diagrams often show the mRNA threading between the subunits, which does not settle the question. mRNA binds to the small subunit of the ribosome, and two tRNAs can bind simultaneously to the large subunit, which holds them so that a peptide bond can form between the amino acid on one and the polypeptide on the other.
items.specStatementText: What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
items.random_wrong: The mRNA binds to the small subunit, and only one tRNA can bind to the large subunit at any moment.

items.q: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?
items.correct: It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
items.misconception: It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
items.why: The codon is described as 'coding for' the amino acid, so students imagine the codon instructing the tRNA what to fetch. Diagrams show the amino acid arriving on the tRNA but rarely show when it was attached. Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid, attached before translation, and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid. Complementary base pairing between the codon and the anticodon ensures that the amino acid delivered is the one the codon specifies.
items.specStatementText: What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
items.random_wrong: It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.

items.q: The start codon on an mRNA molecule is AUG. Which tRNA anticodon binds to this codon, and how is it held there?
items.correct: UAC, held to the codon by hydrogen bonds
items.misconception: TAC, with thymine pairing to adenine
items.why: The pairing rules are drilled for DNA replication (A with T) and applied automatically to any complementary strand. RNA is met later, as a variant of DNA, and its different base is easily forgotten when working under time pressure. RNA nucleotides never contain thymine. In transcription, adenine on the DNA template strand pairs with uracil on the RNA strand, so the transcript contains uracil wherever the template has adenine.
items.specStatementText: Codon and anticodon pair by complementary bases
items.random_wrong: AUG, the same three bases as the codon

items.q: Why does the genetic code use codons of three bases rather than two?
items.correct: Three bases give 64 possible codons, enough for 20 amino acids, whereas two bases give only 16.
items.misconception: Two bases would give 16 codons, which is close enough to 20 for nearly all the amino acids to be coded.
items.why: The triplet code is presented as a fact to memorize rather than as a necessity, so students never do the arithmetic. Some carry a one-to-one picture from GCSE in which 'a base codes for an amino acid'. A triplet code is the shortest that can specify 20 amino acids with 4 bases: 4 × 4 = 16 is too few, whereas 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 is more than enough. Every codon is exactly three bases long.
items.specStatementText: Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
items.random_wrong: Three bases allow each codon to code for up to three different amino acids whenever these are needed.

items.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?
items.correct: Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
items.misconception: A single codon can code for two or more different amino acids.
items.why: In everyday English 'degenerate' suggests something decayed or unreliable, and the direction of the many-to-one relationship is easily reversed when it is first met. Students may also expect a codon to have several meanings because 64 codons seem too many for 20 amino acids. Degeneracy is the feature that several codons can code for the same amino acid, for example GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine. The code is unambiguous: a given codon always specifies the same amino acid.
items.specStatementText: Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
items.random_wrong: The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms.

items.q: The gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria, which then translate it into a polypeptide with the same amino acid sequence as the polypeptide made in human cells. Which feature of the genetic code makes this possible?
items.correct: Universality: the bacterium's tRNAs assign exactly the same amino acids to the codons as human cells do.
items.misconception: Universality: bacteria and humans have the same genes, so the bacterium already had an insulin gene.
items.why: 'Universal' is heard as 'everything is the same', and the difference between sharing a code (the meaning of codons) and sharing the message (the genes) is subtle. Degeneracy and universality are learned together as a pair of unfamiliar terms and are easily interchanged. Universality refers to the code, not the genes: organisms have different genes, but the codons in their mRNA are read as the same amino acids. This is why a human gene inserted into a bacterium is translated into the human protein.
items.specStatementText: Why the code uses triplets, and what degenerate and universal mean
items.random_wrong: Degeneracy: each codon can be read as several amino acids, so the bacterium can make any protein.

items.q: Part of an mRNA molecule, written in the order in which it is translated, has the base sequence AUGGGCAACAGA. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine, GGC glycine, AAC asparagine, AGA arginine, UAC tyrosine, CCG proline, UUG leucine, UCU serine, UGG tryptophan, GCA alanine, ACA threonine. Which amino acid is the third in the polypeptide?
items.correct: asparagine
items.misconception: arginine
items.why: AUG is labelled 'start' in the code table and in diagrams, and start signals in other contexts do not form part of the message. Students therefore treat it like a stop codon in reverse. AUG is both the start codon and the codon for methionine. When deducing an amino acid sequence from an mRNA, the start codon contributes methionine as the first amino acid.
items.specStatementText: Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
items.random_wrong: leucine

items.q: An mRNA molecule has the base sequence AUGUUUGCUUAAGGC, read from the first base. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine (start), UUU phenylalanine, GCU alanine, UAA stop, GGC glycine. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide translated from it?
items.correct: three amino acids
items.misconception: four amino acids
items.why: The code table lists 'stop' in the same cells as the amino acids, so it looks like one more entry to translate. Students also assume that a sequence given in a question is translated in full, from first base to last. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons: no tRNA carries an amino acid for them. When one is reached, translation stops, so the number of amino acids equals the number of codons before the stop codon.
items.specStatementText: Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
items.random_wrong: two amino acids

items.q: How is the polypeptide chain lengthened during translation?
items.correct: The ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time, and a peptide bond links each new amino acid to the chain.
items.misconception: All the tRNAs first line up along the whole length of the mRNA, and their amino acids are then joined together in one step.
items.why: Textbook diagrams of translation frequently show several tRNAs lined up under a row of codons for clarity. Students take the picture literally and see translation as a single assembly step rather than a stepwise process. The ribosome moves stepwise along the mRNA, one codon at a time. Only two tRNAs are bound at once, and each amino acid is linked to the growing polypeptide by a peptide bond as its tRNA pairs with the codon in the ribosome.
items.specStatementText: Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
items.random_wrong: Each tRNA stays attached to its own amino acid, so the chain is a series of tRNAs joined through their amino acids.

items.q: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?
items.correct: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
items.misconception: Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
items.why: Step-by-step diagrams often show a single tRNA arriving, and the delivery is imagined like a courier dropping off a parcel. Students do not see that the amino acid must be joined to the chain while it is still attached to its tRNA. Two tRNAs bind simultaneously to the large subunit: one holds the growing polypeptide and the other has just brought the next amino acid. The peptide bond forms between them while both are bound, and only then does the first tRNA leave.
items.specStatementText: Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
items.random_wrong: Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.

items.q: In the allele that causes sickle cell anaemia, the sixth codon of the mRNA for the beta chain of haemoglobin is GUG instead of GAG. GAG codes for glutamic acid and GUG codes for valine. What is the effect of this mutation on the protein?
items.correct: Valine replaces glutamic acid at one position, which alters haemoglobin enough for it to form fibres at low oxygen concentrations.
items.misconception: One amino acid out of more than a hundred is changed, too small a difference to alter the structure or function of haemoglobin.
items.why: Students reason proportionally: one part in a hundred is a small change. They have not yet linked the amino acid sequence to folding and to interactions with other molecules, where a single altered side chain can be decisive. A protein's structure and function depend on its exact amino acid sequence. Replacing glutamic acid with valine at one position on the surface of the beta chain makes haemoglobin molecules stick together and form fibres at low oxygen concentrations, distorting the red blood cell.
items.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
items.random_wrong: The reading frame is shifted from the sixth codon onward, so every amino acid after it in the beta chain is different.

items.q: A base substitution in a gene changes an mRNA codon from GGU to GGC. Both codons code for glycine. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
items.correct: There is no effect, because the same amino acid, glycine, is inserted at that position.
items.misconception: Its structure changes, because a different codon is bound to give a different amino acid.
items.why: Mutations are introduced as harmful changes, and examples chosen for teaching (sickle cell) are ones that do alter the protein. Students who have not connected degeneracy to mutation expect a one-to-one link between a changed codon and a changed amino acid. Some base substitutions are silent: the new codon codes for the same amino acid and protein structure is unchanged. Others change one amino acid, which may or may not alter the function of the protein.
items.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
items.random_wrong: Every amino acid after this point changes, because the reading frame has been shifted.

items.q: Two mutations occur near the start of the coding sequence of the same gene, in different cells: in one cell a single base is substituted; in the other a single base is inserted. Which mutation is more likely to change the structure of the protein, and why?
items.correct: The insertion, because it shifts the reading frame so that every codon after it is read differently.
items.misconception: Neither is likely to, because the ribosome recognizes each codon wherever it starts reading.
items.why: In a printed sequence there is nothing to show where the codons begin, and students who have not been shown a sequence with the codons marked off assume any three consecutive bases can be a codon. The reading frame is set by the start codon and the ribosome moves along the mRNA exactly three bases at a time, so each base belongs to one codon only. Reading from the wrong base gives a completely different and wrong amino acid sequence.
items.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
items.random_wrong: Neither is likely to, because each changes only a single base and so can affect at most one amino acid.

items.q: During transcription, RNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3' end of the growing RNA strand. What does this mean for the direction of transcription?
items.correct: The RNA is synthesized 5' to 3' while the template strand is read 3' to 5'.
items.misconception: The RNA is synthesized 5' to 3' and the template strand is read in the same 5' to 3' direction.
items.why: Students forget that the two strands of DNA are antiparallel, or attach the 5' to 3' label to the strand being read rather than to the strand being made. Diagrams that show the RNA emerging alongside the template make the two look parallel. 5' to 3' transcription means the RNA is made from its own 5' end towards its 3' end, because RNA polymerase adds each nucleotide to the free 3' hydroxyl of the growing strand. Since the strands are antiparallel, the template is read from its 3' end to its 5' end.
items.specStatementText: Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
items.random_wrong: The RNA is synthesized 3' to 5', because the 3' end is where the chain is being extended.

items.q: Which statement about the direction of translation is correct?
items.correct: The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 5' end towards its 3' end, so the codon nearest the 5' end is translated first.
items.misconception: The ribosome can begin at either end of the mRNA, since the start codon is recognized wherever it is met.
items.why: At SL, sequences are simply written left to right and the 5' and 3' ends are not named, so nothing suggests that the ends differ. The two ends of a strand look alike in most diagrams. The 5' end and 3' end of a strand are chemically different. Transcription is 5' to 3' and translation is 5' to 3': the ribosome binds near the 5' end of the mRNA and moves towards the 3' end.
items.specStatementText: Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
items.random_wrong: The ribosome moves along the mRNA from its 3' end towards its 5' end, matching the direction the template is read.

items.q: A gene is transcribed in muscle cells but not in skin cells, although the DNA of the two cell types is identical. Which statement explains this in terms of initiation of transcription at the promoter?
items.correct: Muscle cells contain transcription factors that bind to the promoter, allowing RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription; skin cells lack them.
items.misconception: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter by itself in both cell types, so the difference between the two cell types must arise at a stage after transcription.
items.why: The SL description of transcription features only RNA polymerase, and diagrams show it binding directly to DNA. Transcription factors are added later as extras, so they are seen as optional accelerators rather than as a requirement. Transcription factors that bind to the promoter are needed for RNA polymerase to bind and begin transcription in eukaryotes. Which genes a cell transcribes therefore depends on which transcription factors it contains.
items.specStatementText: Transcription starts at the promoter, once transcription factors bind
items.random_wrong: In muscle cells the promoter is transcribed as the first part of the mRNA, and this acts as a signal for the gene to be expressed.

items.q: Which statement about non-coding sequences in eukaryotic DNA is correct?
items.correct: The genes for tRNA and rRNA are transcribed, but their RNA products are never translated into polypeptides.
items.misconception: Non-coding sequences such as introns and telomeres have no function at all and so are never transcribed into RNA.
items.why: The popular phrase 'junk DNA' and the GCSE definition of a gene as 'a section of DNA that codes for a protein' together suggest that anything not coding for protein does nothing. 'Non-coding' is heard as 'non-functional'. Non-coding sequences do not code for polypeptides, but many are functional: promoters and other regulators control transcription, telomeres protect chromosome ends, introns are transcribed and removed, and rRNA and tRNA genes are transcribed into functional RNA.
items.specStatementText: Most eukaryotic DNA does not code for polypeptides, but has functions
items.random_wrong: Every gene codes for a polypeptide, so tRNA and rRNA are both produced by translation of their own mRNA molecules.

items.q: A eukaryotic gene contains three exons separated by two introns. Which statement describes the mature mRNA produced from this gene?
items.correct: It contains the three exons joined together, with a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail added on.
items.misconception: It contains the three exons only, because the introns were cut out of the DNA before the gene was transcribed.
items.why: Introns are described as 'removed' and students picture the removal happening on the gene, the thing they think of as containing introns. Cutting DNA seems no different from cutting RNA to a student who has not separated the two molecules. Post-transcriptional modification acts on the RNA transcript, not on the DNA. RNA polymerase transcribes the whole gene, introns included, and splicing then removes the introns from the pre-mRNA in the nucleus.
items.specStatementText: Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
items.random_wrong: It contains the two introns joined together, because the exons were the sections removed by splicing.

items.q: What is the role of the 5' cap and the 3' poly-A tail added to a eukaryotic mRNA transcript?
items.correct: They stabilize the mRNA, protecting it from being broken down before it is translated.
items.misconception: They are translated, adding a short run of extra amino acids to each end of the polypeptide.
items.why: Students learn that mRNA is read as codons and assume anything on the mRNA is code. The poly-A tail, being a sequence of bases, looks like a run of AAA codons for lysine. The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail are added after transcription to stabilize the mRNA transcript. Translation begins at the start codon and ends at a stop codon, so the cap and the tail lie outside the sequence that is translated.
items.specStatementText: Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
items.random_wrong: They mark the positions of the introns so that the splicing enzymes know which sections to remove.

items.q: The human genome contains about 20 000 protein-coding genes, yet human cells produce well over 20 000 different polypeptides. Which process accounts for this?
items.correct: Alternative splicing, in which different combinations of exons from one pre-mRNA are joined to give different mature mRNAs.
items.misconception: Mutation of the gene during transcription, so that each transcript carries a slightly different base sequence.
items.why: 'Mutation' is used loosely to mean any error or change, and talk of 'mutant proteins' suggests the change happened to the protein. Students who know that replication can make copying errors extend the idea to every copying step. Mutations that change protein structure are changes in the DNA base sequence of the gene, so every mRNA transcribed from the mutated gene, and every polypeptide translated from it, carries the same change.
items.specStatementText: One gene can give several polypeptides by splicing exons differently
items.random_wrong: Degeneracy of the genetic code, which allows a codon to be translated as different amino acids in different cells.

items.q: Which sequence of events initiates translation of an mRNA in a eukaryotic cell?
items.correct: The small subunit binds to the 5' end of the mRNA and moves to the start codon; the initiator tRNA binds there; then the large subunit attaches.
items.misconception: The complete ribosome binds directly to the start codon as a single unit, and the initiator tRNA then enters the ribosome and pairs with the codon.
items.why: Ribosomes are drawn as one blob sitting on the mRNA, and in the SL account there is no need to separate the subunits. Students also expect binding to occur at the start codon because that is where translation starts. Initiation of translation begins with attachment of the small subunit to the 5' terminal of the mRNA. It moves along to the start codon, the initiator tRNA binds, and only then does the large subunit attach to complete the ribosome.
items.specStatementText: How translation starts, and the A, P and E sites
items.random_wrong: The small subunit binds to the 3' end of the mRNA and moves along until it reaches the start codon, where the large subunit attaches.

items.q: During elongation, what are the roles of the A, P and E sites of the ribosome?
items.correct: A tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters the A site, the tRNA holding the growing polypeptide is in the P site, and a used tRNA leaves from the E site.
items.misconception: A tRNA enters the ribosome at the E site, moves to the P site where its amino acid is added to the growing chain, and finally leaves the ribosome from the A site.
items.why: The letters A, P and E are learned before their names, and 'E' is a natural abbreviation for entry. The correct names (aminoacyl, peptidyl, exit) are unfamiliar words that do not stick. The A site accepts the incoming tRNA carrying an amino acid, the P site holds the tRNA attached to the growing polypeptide, and the E (exit) site holds the tRNA that has given up its amino acid just before it leaves.
items.specStatementText: How translation starts, and the A, P and E sites
items.random_wrong: Only one site is occupied at any one time: a tRNA enters the A site, passes through the P site and then the E site, and leaves before the next tRNA enters.

items.q: Insulin consists of two polypeptide chains, A and B, held together by disulfide bonds, yet it is coded for by a single gene. How is functional insulin produced?
items.correct: Pre-proinsulin loses its signal sequence to give proinsulin; a central section is then cut out, leaving the two chains.
items.misconception: Two separate polypeptides, A and B, are translated from the gene and are then joined to each other by disulfide bonds in the Golgi apparatus.
items.why: Insulin is shown as two chains, and the simplest explanation of two chains is two separate polypeptides. Students who know that proteins can contain several polypeptides (such as haemoglobin) assume the same here. Insulin is coded for by one gene and made as one polypeptide, pre-proinsulin. Removal of the signal sequence gives proinsulin; removal of a central section then leaves the two chains, already linked by disulfide bonds that formed while they were one molecule.
items.specStatementText: Many polypeptides are cut or altered before they work
items.random_wrong: The polypeptide made by translation is already insulin, and the two chains form as it folds when it leaves the ribosome.

items.q: Why does a cell continually break down some of its proteins in proteasomes while synthesizing new ones?
items.correct: Sustaining a functional proteome needs constant turnover: proteins no longer needed are removed and their amino acids reused.
items.misconception: Proteins are permanent once they have been made, so proteasomes act only when a cell has been badly damaged or is about to die.
items.why: Proteins are introduced as structural components and enzymes that a cell 'has', like parts of a machine, and breakdown is met only in the context of damage or digestion. The constant turnover of the proteome is invisible in a healthy cell. Proteasomes break down proteins that are no longer needed or are damaged, releasing amino acids that are recycled into new proteins. This turnover is continuous and is required to keep the proteome functional as the cell's needs change.
items.specStatementText: Proteins are constantly broken down and rebuilt
items.random_wrong: Proteasomes break down proteins only when the cell is short of glucose and needs amino acids as a source of energy.

items.q: How much of a cell's DNA is transcribed when a gene is expressed?
items.correct: Only one strand of the section of DNA making up that gene is transcribed, producing an RNA copy of that gene alone.
items.misconception: Transcription copies the whole DNA molecule, or both strands of the gene, in the same way that replication does.
items.why: Transcription is met straight after replication, in which the whole molecule and both strands are copied, and the word 'copy' is used for both processes. Diagrams that show RNA polymerase opening the double helix look like the replication fork. Transcription is the synthesis of RNA using a DNA template: one strand of one gene is used as the template, and the product is a single RNA strand complementary to it. Both DNA strands are left unchanged and re-pair once the RNA is released.
items.specStatementText: Transcription: RNA polymerase makes an RNA copy of one gene
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which DNA base on the template strand does uracil pair with during transcription?
items.correct: Adenine: wherever the template strand has A, the RNA strand has U.
items.misconception: Uracil is 'the RNA version of thymine', so it is placed opposite thymine on the template strand, and adenine on the template is matched by adenine on the RNA.
items.why: The rule 'RNA has U instead of T' is learned as a substitution of one letter for another, so students place U wherever they see T. They do not go back to the pairing rules, in which U takes over thymine's role of pairing with adenine, not thymine's position. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA and takes over its pairing partner: adenine (A) on the DNA template strand pairs with uracil (U) on the RNA strand, and thymine on the template pairs with adenine on the RNA.
items.specStatementText: Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a cell that will never divide again still need to conserve its DNA base sequence?
items.correct: Yes. A non-dividing somatic cell transcribes its DNA for the rest of its life, so its sequences must be conserved for as long as the cell lives.
items.misconception: DNA only matters when it is being copied, so a cell that never replicates its DNA again does not need its base sequence to be preserved.
items.why: DNA is met mainly in the context of replication and inheritance, so its importance is tied to being passed on. The continuous use of DNA as the template for transcription in a living cell is less visible than its copying at division. In somatic cells that do not divide, such as neurons, the same DNA is the template for all transcription throughout the life of the cell, so its base sequences must be conserved for the life of the cell, which may be many decades.
items.specStatementText: A DNA template can be read again and again without changing
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At which stage is the expression of a gene most commonly switched on or off?
items.correct: At transcription, the first stage: a gene that is not transcribed produces no mRNA and so no polypeptide.
items.misconception: Whether a gene is expressed is decided at translation, not transcription: a gene is 'off' if its mRNA is not translated or if its protein is broken down, and transcription is just a preliminary step that happens automatically.
items.why: Translation is the stage at which the protein is actually made, so students locate the decision about whether to make a protein there. Transcription seems a preliminary step that happens automatically. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression and is a key stage at which the expression of a gene can be switched on and off. Switching off transcription prevents the mRNA from being made at all, so nothing is wasted on producing a polypeptide that is not needed.
items.specStatementText: Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where do the amino acids in a polypeptide come from during translation?
items.correct: From the pool of free amino acids in the cytoplasm; each is brought to the ribosome by a tRNA and joined to the chain.
items.misconception: The ribosome makes amino acids by converting the bases of the mRNA into amino acids.
items.why: Translation is described as 'converting' the mRNA sequence into an amino acid sequence, which is heard as a chemical conversion of one molecule into another. Simplified diagrams show amino acids appearing at the ribosome without showing where they came from. The base sequence of mRNA determines the order in which amino acids are joined, but the amino acids themselves already exist in the cytoplasm. Each tRNA carries an amino acid to the ribosome, where it is added to the polypeptide.
items.specStatementText: Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does translation take place?
items.correct: On ribosomes in the cytoplasm (free, or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum), after the mRNA has left the nucleus.
items.misconception: Translation takes place in the nucleus, next to the DNA, because that is where the gene is.
items.why: Transcription and translation are often drawn in one continuous diagram, and the nucleus is where the process starts. Students do not register that mRNA leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores before it is translated. Transcription takes place in the nucleus, but the mRNA then passes into the cytoplasm, where ribosomes translate it into a polypeptide. Ribosomes are not found inside the nucleus.
items.specStatementText: Translation: a ribosome turns mRNA codons into a polypeptide
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the genetic code table be read directly from a DNA template strand sequence?
items.correct: No. The table lists mRNA codons, so the template sequence must first be converted to the complementary mRNA sequence (with U in place of T).
items.misconception: The code table can be applied straight to the DNA template strand, reading T as U, because tRNA anticodons pair with the gene's DNA.
items.why: Questions often begin from a DNA sequence, and the extra transcription step is easy to skip when the table looks like it takes any sequence of bases. Some students also think tRNAs pair with DNA, having not separated the roles of DNA and mRNA. The genetic code is expressed as a table of mRNA codons. tRNA anticodons pair with mRNA, not DNA, so to deduce the amino acid sequence from a template strand, first write the complementary mRNA sequence and then read its codons from the table.
items.specStatementText: Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What type of bond joins amino acids to each other in the growing polypeptide?
items.correct: A peptide bond: a covalent bond formed by condensation between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next.
items.misconception: The amino acids are held together by hydrogen bonds, like the bonds between the codon and the anticodon.
items.why: Hydrogen bonds are mentioned repeatedly in transcription and translation (between DNA strands, between RNA and template, between codon and anticodon), so students assume they are the bond of the whole topic. The word 'bond' is used for both without the distinction being stressed. Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds, which are covalent and strong, so the polypeptide holds together after it leaves the ribosome. Hydrogen bonds hold the anticodon to the codon temporarily and break when the tRNA leaves.
items.specStatementText: Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to a tRNA after its amino acid has been added to the polypeptide?
items.correct: It leaves the ribosome without its amino acid and can be reloaded with another amino acid and used again.
items.misconception: Each tRNA stays bonded to its amino acid, so the finished polypeptide is a chain of amino acids with their tRNAs still attached.
items.why: Diagrams of elongation show tRNAs beneath the growing chain and the moment of release is easy to miss. Students who see the tRNA as 'delivering' the amino acid do not consider that the bond between them has to break for the tRNA to be free. When the peptide bond forms, the amino acid is transferred from its tRNA to the polypeptide chain. The tRNA that has given up its amino acid leaves the ribosome as the ribosome moves along, and it is reused.
items.specStatementText: Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a base substitution shift the reading frame?
items.correct: No. A substitution replaces one base with another and leaves the number of bases unchanged, so only the codon containing it is altered. Only insertions or deletions shift the reading frame.
items.misconception: Any point mutation, including a substitution, shifts the reading frame so that every codon after it is read differently.
items.why: Substitutions, insertions and deletions are learned in one list, and the dramatic frameshift effect is memorable, so it is attached to all of them. Students do not check whether the number of bases has changed. A substitution changes one codon only, so at most one amino acid is affected. A single-base insertion or deletion changes the grouping of every base after it into codons, altering every subsequent amino acid.
items.specStatementText: A single base change can change a protein
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the promoter part of the mRNA?
items.correct: No. The promoter is a DNA sequence next to the gene where RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind; transcription begins after it, so it is not the start codon and is not copied into the mRNA that is translated.
items.misconception: The promoter is the start codon, or the promoter is transcribed and forms the first part of the mRNA.
items.why: 'Start' is used for both the promoter (where transcription starts) and the start codon (where translation starts), and students merge the two. Diagrams place the promoter at the beginning of the gene, which suggests it is copied along with the rest. Initiation of transcription happens at the promoter, a non-coding DNA sequence adjacent to the gene. RNA polymerase binds there and then transcribes the gene; the promoter itself positions the enzyme and is not the start codon of the mRNA.
items.specStatementText: Transcription starts at the promoter, once transcription factors bind
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How are tRNA and rRNA molecules produced?
items.correct: By transcription of the genes for tRNA and rRNA; the RNA transcripts are the functional products and are never translated.
items.misconception: Every gene codes for a polypeptide, so tRNA and rRNA must be produced by translation, like proteins.
items.why: Genes are defined for students as coding for proteins, and the sequence DNA to mRNA to protein is repeated so often that any gene product is assumed to be a protein. Students may not have met the idea of a gene whose product is an RNA. The genes for rRNAs and tRNAs are examples of non-coding DNA: they are transcribed to produce RNA molecules that function directly in translation, without being translated into polypeptides.
items.specStatementText: Most eukaryotic DNA does not code for polypeptides, but has functions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which sequences are removed by splicing, and which are kept in the mature mRNA?
items.correct: Introns are removed and exons are spliced together and kept.
items.misconception: Exons are the sequences cut out and introns are the sequences kept in the mRNA.
items.why: The names are learned as a pair and their derivations are unhelpful to a student: 'intron' sounds like it should be 'in' the mRNA and 'exon' sounds like it should exit. In fact exons are the expressed sequences. Exons are expressed: they remain in the mature mRNA and are translated. Introns are intervening sequences within the gene, transcribed but then removed by splicing.
items.specStatementText: Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does each gene code for exactly one polypeptide?
items.correct: No. In eukaryotes, alternative splicing allows one gene to code for several different polypeptides, so there are far more polypeptides than protein-coding genes.
items.misconception: Each gene codes for exactly one polypeptide, so an organism needs a separate gene for every different polypeptide it makes.
items.why: The 'one gene, one polypeptide' idea is a useful simplification that is taught early and stated as a rule. It is reinforced by every worked example, which uses one gene and one product. Splicing together different combinations of exons allows one gene to code for different polypeptides. The human genome has about 20 000 protein-coding genes but produces many more different polypeptides.
items.specStatementText: One gene can give several polypeptides by splicing exons differently
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does alternative splicing change the base sequence of the gene, and is it what produces the separate chains of a protein such as insulin?
items.correct: No to both. Alternative splicing recombines exons of the pre-mRNA, leaving the gene unchanged; the two chains of insulin come from cutting one polypeptide after translation.
items.misconception: Alternative splicing is a kind of mutation that alters the gene, or it is what must be responsible whenever one gene gives rise to more than one polypeptide chain.
items.why: 'Variants' sounds like 'mutants', and having just learned that alternative splicing lets one gene give several polypeptides, students apply it to every case of one gene and several chains, including the post-translational cutting of proinsulin. Alternative splicing produces different mature mRNAs from one gene without changing the DNA. Insulin's two chains are not splice variants: they are two parts of one polypeptide from which the central section has been removed after translation.
items.specStatementText: One gene can give several polypeptides by splicing exons differently
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a polypeptide functional as soon as it leaves the ribosome?
items.correct: Often not. Many polypeptides must be modified first, for example by having sections removed, forming disulfide bonds or having groups added.
items.misconception: Translation makes the finished protein, so a polypeptide works as soon as it has been released from the ribosome.
items.why: The pathway is taught as 'DNA to mRNA to protein', with translation as the final step, so there seems to be nothing after it. Insulin diagrams usually show the finished two-chain hormone, not the single chain it was made from. Many polypeptides must be modified before they can function. Pre-proinsulin, the polypeptide made by translation, has to have its signal sequence removed and then a central section cut out before it becomes active insulin.
items.specStatementText: Many polypeptides are cut or altered before they work
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When does a cell break down its proteins in proteasomes?
items.correct: Continuously, in normal conditions, as part of maintaining a functional proteome; not only when it is short of nutrients.
items.misconception: Proteins are broken down only when the cell is starved and needs their amino acids as a source of energy.
items.why: At GCSE, protein breakdown is met as the body 'using muscle protein' during starvation, so students see it as an emergency measure. The idea that breakdown is a routine part of regulating which proteins are present is new. Sustaining a functional proteome requires constant protein breakdown and synthesis. Proteasomes remove proteins that are no longer needed so that the amino acids can be reused, whatever the cell's energy supply.
items.specStatementText: Proteins are constantly broken down and rebuilt
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to the amino acids released when a proteasome breaks down a protein?
items.correct: They are recycled: they return to the cell's pool of free amino acids and are used to synthesize new proteins.
items.misconception: Amino acids released by protein breakdown are waste and are excreted, as urea, from the cell.
items.why: GCSE teaches that excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver and excreted as urea, so any amino acid produced by breakdown is assumed to be on its way out. The recycling of amino acids within a cell is not covered until this topic. Recycling of amino acids by proteasomes means the amino acids from broken-down proteins are reused in translation. Constant breakdown and synthesis together sustain the proteome without the cell needing a fresh supply of every amino acid.
items.specStatementText: Proteins are constantly broken down and rebuilt
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If RNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the 3' end of the RNA, is the RNA being synthesized 3' to 5'?
items.correct: No. Adding to the 3' end means the strand grows from its 5' end towards its 3' end, which is 5' to 3' synthesis.
items.misconception: The direction of synthesis is named after the end that is being extended, so a strand that grows at its 3' end is being made '3' to 5''.
items.why: The phrase 'added at the 3' end' puts the 3' first in the student's mind, and the convention that direction is named from the first nucleotide made to the last is rarely stated explicitly. Students also confuse the end being extended with the direction of movement of the enzyme along the template. 5' to 3' synthesis means the first nucleotide of the RNA is its 5' end and each new nucleotide is joined to the free 3' hydroxyl group, so the 3' end is where growth happens and the strand is built 5' to 3'. The same convention applies to DNA replication.
items.specStatementText: Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
